keyVerseText: After him repaired Meremoth the son of Urijah the son of Koz another piece, from the door of the house of Eliashib even to the end of the house of Eliashib.
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun תַּכְלִית (taklîyth) derives from the root כָּלָה (kâlâh), which conveys the idea of bringing something to its end, completion, or fulfillment. This root encompasses concepts such as finishing, ceasing, or accomplishing a task fully. Thus, the literal sense of תַּכְלִית goes beyond a mere 'end' to include the notion of perfect completion or consummation, highlighting not just termination but the achievement of a full and intended purpose.
usageInScripture: The word תַּכְלִית appears five times in Scripture and is consistently translated with terms emphasizing completion or finality, such as 'even to the end,' 'unto perfection,' and 'come to an end.' This range of translations reveals a consistent semantic field centered on the idea of reaching a boundary or achieving full completeness. Whether referring to physical boundaries, like in Nehemiah 3:21, or metaphorical or spiritual ends, the term conveys a thoroughness or consummation that is both spatial and qualitative.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תַּכְלִית as both 'end' and 'completion' enriches our grasp of God's redemptive work and promises in Scripture. It reminds believers that God's purposes are not haphazard or partial but are brought to perfect fulfillment in Christ. The concept of consummation points to the ultimate completion of salvation and sanctification, assuring Christians that God will bring His work in them and in creation to its intended glorious conclusion. This word encourages faith in the certainty and perfection of God's divine plan.
keyVerseReflection: In Nehemiah 3:21, the phrase 'even to the end of the house of Eliashib' uses תַּכְלִית to mark the physical boundary of a repair project, emphasizing thoroughness and completeness in the work. The word here conveys not just a spatial limit but the idea that the task was carried out fully, leaving nothing unfinished. This reflects a principle applicable to spiritual life: God’s work in His people is intended to be complete and perfect, extending fully to its appointed end.
